analysis.one_liner: Toughens enforcement of water pollution permits with minimum fines and mandatory inspections of repeat violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in October 1991 with one sponsor and four cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted a documented gap in water pollution enforcement: many facilities with Clean Water Act permits were violating them, and the fines they paid were often smaller than the money they saved by polluting. It would have required penalties to at least cover a violator's economic gain plus interest, set minimum fines for serious and repeat violations, banned negotiating those minimums down, required inspections of repeat violators, adjusted penalties for inflation, expanded the public's right to sue polluters, and empowered city sewage plants to inspect and fine industrial dischargers.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink, fish in, or use the nation's waters — the bill's own findings state that permit violations 'harm users of such water system.' Law-abiding facilities that already pay to comply would also benefit by no longer competing against violators that save money by polluting.

how_it_helps.text: Requires civil penalties to be at least the economic benefit or savings a violator gained from the violation, plus interest from the date of the violation, so breaking the rules can no longer pay [S2] [S3].

Sets minimum fines of $1,000 for a first serious discharge violation and $5,000 for repeat or significant violations, bars those minimums from being compromised or reduced, and adjusts all penalty amounts for inflation [S2] [S3].
Requires EPA to inspect facilities run by 'significant noncompliers' and to publish an annual public list of them and their violations [S2] [S3].

Expands citizen lawsuits to cover pretreatment and local-limit violations and lets anyone who uses water downstream from a discharge sue, while allowing courts to direct civil penalty money to environmental mitigation projects [S2] [S3].
Requires random, independent-laboratory inspections of permitted discharges and monthly discharge reports signed by the facility's top official, who becomes responsible for their accuracy [S3].
Lets city-owned sewage treatment plants inspect industrial users and assess civil penalties against them, closing an enforcement gap at the local level [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial and municipal facilities that discharge pollutants under Clean Water Act permits — they face higher fines, mandatory inspections, more frequent monitoring reports, and criminal liability for violating local pretreatment rules. Some of those compliance costs could be passed to consumers and local ratepayers.

drawbacks.text: Publicly owned treatment works are covered too: states would have to give city sewage plants inspection and penalty authority, and municipal violators would face the same minimum fines — costs ultimately borne by local ratepayers [S2] [S3].

The bill extends recordkeeping, reporting, and inspection requirements to 'any person subject to a requirement of this Act,' not just point-source permittees, adding paperwork and inspection burdens across the regulated community [S2] [S3].

It repeals the provision treating a single operational upset that breaks multiple pollution limits at once as one violation, meaning an equipment malfunction could count as several separate violations — a harsher outcome for facilities facing genuine accidents [S2] [S3].
Higher, inflation-adjusted penalties raise the cost of doing business for dischargers, and some of that cost can be expected to reach consumers through prices and utility rates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented problem — its findings state that EPA penalties were often smaller than the money violators saved, which penalizes facilities that obey the law [S3]. The enforcement teeth (economic-benefit recovery, minimum fines, mandatory inspections, citizen suits) directly protect water quality and public health. The main costs are compliance burdens and fines falling partly on publicly owned utilities, and a stricter counting of violations from single operational upsets. On balance it was a pro-enforcement bill whose costs fell mostly on regulated dischargers rather than on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on October 22, 1991, and the committee never acted on it before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg (D-NJ), joined by Senator Daniel Moynihan (D-NY), introduced the bill on October 22, 1991 [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
No committee action, floor action, or vote followed; the complete action history ends with the referral to committee [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that violate their water pollution permits are better off, because the bill would have imposed minimum fines equal to their economic gain from violating, mandatory inspections, and a published list of repeat violators. EPA and state agencies also avoided new inspection, reporting, and annual-list obligations.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill died in committee without a vote or recorded opposition, so no party split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (chemical plants, factories, and other permitted point sources)
industries.note: The bill raised penalties above what violations earned, set minimum fines for serious and repeat violations, banned negotiating those minimums down, and required random independent inspections and monthly reports — the costs of an enforcement regime that its own findings said was letting violators profit [S2] [S3]. Its interest in blocking or weakening it runs against public access to clean water.

industries.industry: Municipal wastewater utilities (publicly owned treatment works)
industries.note: They would gain new authority to inspect and fine industrial users that discharge into their systems, but they also face minimum penalties for their own violations and new monthly reporting duties, with costs passed to local ratepayers [S2] [S3].

The bill's expanded citizen-suit rights (including downstream water users) and mitigation funding from penalties would have strengthened public and environmental enforcement tools that never materialized [S2] [S3].
